title: 研究解读｜手写笔记与记忆
sub: 仔细阅读 Section C 实战 · 博浩原创真题风格长文 · 教育话题

data.passage:
Walk into any university lecture hall and you will see rows of students typing busily on laptops, their eyes fixed on glowing screens. A team of researchers at Stanford University has now added new evidence to the debate, asking a question that is easier to pose than to answer: Whether taking notes by hand helps students remember material better than typing them. Their findings, published in PNAS, offer one of the clearest answers so far.
The team set out to settle the question with evidence rather than opinion, gathering data over a substantial period. When the data were analysed, a clear pattern appeared. After a lecture, the researchers tested both groups and found that the students who wrote by hand recalled about 42% more factual detail a week later, even though the typists had produced far more words. To make sure the comparison was fair, the team controlled for factors such as background and daily habits.
Why would such a difference appear? Writing by hand forces the brain to summarize and rephrase information as it is heard, a process of deeper processing that typing, which often amounts to transcription, does not require. The explanation fits with a wider body of research on how the mind works.
Not everyone thinks the effect is as straightforward as it first appears. Typing remains useful when the goal is simply to record large amounts of information quickly, and the advantage of handwriting appears to shrink when students are given time to review their notes afterwards. Taken together, the evidence paints a more balanced picture than headlines suggest. The authors are careful to describe their results as strong evidence rather than final proof.
What does this mean in practice? Students who want to remember lecture material should put away their laptops for key parts of the class and write out their notes by hand instead. In a busy world, such small adjustments can add up to real change over time. And that is a conclusion worth acting on, whatever side of the debate one starts from.

opts: Whether frequent standing breaks can offset the health risks of long periods of sitting.

Reviewing dozens of clinical trials involving thousands of patients, the researchers found that those who listened to music during procedures reported about 53% lower pain scores and needed noticeably less pain medication than those who did not.

title: 午间散步与创造力：一项新研究给出的答案
sub: 仔细阅读 Section C 实战 · 博浩原创真题风格长文 · 健康话题

data.passage:
Many employees spend their lunch break scrolling through their phones at their desks, yet a growing number of companies are now urging staff to step outside instead. How much does it really matter? A group of researchers at MIT set out to examine a familiar but surprisingly unresolved question: Whether short walks during the working day can boost creative thinking. What the team discovered, described in detail in The Lancet Public Health, is worth the attention of anyone who faces this situation regularly.
To examine the issue, the researchers collected information over time and compared the outcomes with unusual care. When the data were analysed, a clear pattern appeared. Over a six-week trial, employees who were asked to take a ten-minute walk every two hours produced about 33% more original ideas in a standard creativity test than colleagues who remained seated, and they also reported feeling less mentally exhausted. Additional checks ruled out the most obvious alternative explanations.
Why would such a difference appear? Moderate exercise increases blood flow to the brain and, just as importantly, gives the mind regular breaks from focused attention, and both effects appear to help people see problems from fresh angles. It is a reminder that apparently small choices can have surprisingly large effects.
Not everyone thinks the effect is as straightforward as it first appears. The benefit was weakest on days when participants were already highly active, which suggests that the gains come less from extra exercise than from the deliberate pause it provides. Taken together, the evidence paints a more balanced picture than headlines suggest. As always, one study alone rarely settles a question for good.
What does this mean in practice? Managers should treat short walks not as lost working time but as an investment in their employees' thinking, and workers themselves should protect those breaks from meetings. The study is a useful reminder that everyday habits matter more than we often assume. And that is a conclusion worth acting on, whatever side of the debate one starts from.

title: 关于手机通知与专注力的新证据
sub: 仔细阅读 Section C 实战 · 博浩原创真题风格长文 · 科技话题

data.passage:
A smartphone buzzes on the desk, and within seconds the owner has abandoned a report, a conversation or a book to check the screen. How much does it really matter? A group of researchers at the University of British Columbia set out to examine a familiar but surprisingly unresolved question: How ordinary phone notifications affect people's ability to concentrate on demanding tasks. Their findings, published in the British Medical Journal, offer one of the clearest answers so far.
The team set out to settle the question with evidence rather than opinion, gathering data over a substantial period. The results pointed in one direction and were supported by more than one measure. In a controlled experiment, participants who received just three notifications an hour made about 46% more errors on a concentration task than those who switched their phones to silent, even though they were not allowed to open the apps that had sent the alerts. The pattern held even after the researchers took other possible explanations into account.
The researchers believe they know why. Every notification forces the brain to perform a small mental shift, and researchers believe these shifts, repeated dozens of times a day, steadily drain the limited pool of attention available for deep work. It is a reminder that apparently small choices can have surprisingly large effects.
There is, however, another side to the story. The same study found that people quickly adapted when they disabled notifications permanently, which suggests that the problem is not the phone itself but the habits built around it. The researchers stress that the results should be applied with care. For that reason, sweeping conclusions should be treated with caution.
So what should ordinary readers take away from the study? People who need to focus should turn off non-essential alerts and schedule short, deliberate periods for checking messages rather than responding to each one as it arrives. Whether the change is worth making now seems easier to answer than it did before. The evidence, in short, gives people a practical reason to change how they go about their daily routines.

title: 关于城市屋顶绿化的新证据
sub: 仔细阅读 Section C 实战 · 博浩原创真题风格长文 · 环境话题

data.passage:
From the air, many city centres appear as grey grids of concrete and glass, but a quiet transformation is taking place on their rooftops. How much does it really matter? A group of researchers at the University of Hong Kong set out to examine a familiar but surprisingly unresolved question: Whether rooftop gardens can meaningfully cool cities and reduce energy use. What the team discovered, described in detail in the Journal of Applied Psychology, is worth the attention of anyone who faces this situation regularly.
To examine the issue, the researchers collected information over time and compared the outcomes with unusual care. When the data were analysed, a clear pattern appeared. Analysing temperature records from more than a hundred city blocks over three summers, the team found that buildings with green roofs stayed up to 8 degrees cooler in peak heat and used noticeably less electricity for air conditioning. The pattern held even after the researchers took other possible explanations into account.
Why would such a difference appear? Plants cool the air through evaporation and shade, and a layer of soil on a roof also slows the transfer of heat into the building below during the hottest hours of the day. The explanation fits with a wider body of research on how the mind works.
Not everyone thinks the effect is as straightforward as it first appears. Green roofs are expensive to install and need regular watering in dry spells, so researchers caution that they work best as one part of a wider strategy that includes street trees and lighter-coloured surfaces. Taken together, the evidence paints a more balanced picture than headlines suggest. As always, one study alone rarely settles a question for good.
What does this mean in practice? City planners should encourage green roofs on large new buildings and pair them with rainwater collection systems that reduce the cost of keeping the gardens alive. Whether the change is worth making now seems easier to answer than it did before. In the end, the research suggests that small, deliberate habits can shape outcomes more than most people assume.

For more than a century the five-day working week has been treated as a natural rhythm of modern life, yet a wave of experiments is now questioning that assumption. A team of researchers at Yale University has now added new evidence to the debate, asking a question that is easier to pose than to answer: Whether moving to a four-day week can maintain productivity while improving well-being. What the team discovered, described in detail in the American Economic Review, is worth the attention of anyone who faces this situation regularly.

To make sure the comparison was fair, the team controlled for factors such as background and daily habits.

The findings also come with important caveats. The model works best in jobs where output can be measured clearly, and some managers warn that in client-facing roles a four-day week simply squeezes the same workload into fewer days. Taken together, the evidence paints a more balanced picture than headlines suggest. For that reason, sweeping conclusions should be treated with caution.
So what should ordinary readers take away from the study? Firms considering shorter hours should start with a pilot, measure outcomes carefully, and involve employees in deciding which tasks can be dropped rather than compressed. The study is a useful reminder that everyday habits matter more than we often assume. In the end, the research suggests that small, deliberate habits can shape outcomes more than most people assume.

title: 关于睡眠与情绪记忆的新证据
sub: 仔细阅读 Section C 实战 · 博浩原创真题风格长文 · 心理话题

data.passage:
Students facing an important exam often cut their sleep to a few hours, convinced that every extra minute of study is precious. For years the answer has remained surprisingly unclear, so researchers at ETH Zurich designed a careful study around a single question: How a single night of poor sleep affects the way people remember emotional events. The results, reported in The Lancet Public Health, may force many people to reconsider long-held assumptions.
To answer the question, the researchers designed a study that compared two situations as closely as possible. The differences that emerged were consistent and difficult to explain away. In the study, participants who were kept awake for one night remembered about 18% more of the negative details from a set of stories than well-rested participants, but they forgot the neutral details far more quickly. Additional checks ruled out the most obvious alternative explanations.
Why would such a difference appear? Sleep appears to help the brain file emotional memories into their proper context, and without that overnight processing, negative images stay vivid and keep intruding into conscious thought. It is a reminder that apparently small choices can have surprisingly large effects.
There is, however, another side to the story. The effect may be protective in the short term because people are primed to notice danger, but researchers warn that chronic poor sleep can leave individuals trapped in an anxious, negatively biased view of their own past. Taken together, the evidence paints a more balanced picture than headlines suggest. The authors are careful to describe their results as strong evidence rather than final proof.
So what should ordinary readers take away from the study? Students who want to keep their mood steady during revision should treat seven to eight hours of sleep as part of their study plan, not as time stolen from it. Whether the change is worth making now seems easier to answer than it did before. In the end, the research suggests that small, deliberate habits can shape outcomes more than most people assume.

data.passage:
Video games hold the attention of young people for hours, and educators have long wondered whether that engagement can be borrowed for the classroom. For years the answer has remained surprisingly unclear, so researchers at the University of Hong Kong designed a careful study around a single question: Whether game-like elements genuinely improve learning or merely entertain. What the team discovered, described in detail in the journal Nature Human Behaviour, is worth the attention of anyone who faces this situation regularly.
The team set out to settle the question with evidence rather than opinion, gathering data over a substantial period. The differences that emerged were consistent and difficult to explain away. Across a review of more than forty studies, students who learned with well-designed game elements scored about 51% higher on tests of the material than those taught in the usual way, and they also reported greater motivation to keep practising. The pattern held even after the researchers took other possible explanations into account.
The researchers believe they know why. Games work by giving immediate feedback, clear goals and a sense of progress, all of which keep learners in a state of focused effort that traditional exercises often fail to create. Similar mechanisms have been identified in other settings as well.
Not everyone thinks the effect is as straightforward as it first appears. The researchers warn that points and badges alone change nothing, since shallow rewards can even distract from learning when they are not tied to the difficulty of the material. Taken together, the evidence paints a more balanced picture than headlines suggest. The authors are careful to describe their results as strong evidence rather than final proof.
So what should ordinary readers take away from the study? Teachers should use game elements that reward understanding and effort, such as levels based on mastery, rather than simple speed or luck-based prizes. The study is a useful reminder that everyday habits matter more than we often assume. And that is a conclusion worth acting on, whatever side of the debate one starts from.

qs.q: What question does the passage set out to answer?
opts: Whether spacing out study sessions over time produces better long-term memory than cramming.
Whether taking notes by hand helps students remember material better than typing them.
How the gig economy has changed the nature of work for delivery riders.
Whether game-like elements genuinely improve learning or merely entertain.
qs.ex: 主旨题。全文围绕「游戏化元素能否真正促进学习」展开，正确项完整概括了这项研究要回答的核心问题。

qs.q: What did the study described in the passage find?
opts: Analysing waste from hundreds of kitchens, the researchers found that about 43% of the food thrown away at home was still perfectly edible, with leftovers and forgotten purchases at the back of the fridge the biggest contributors.

Following more than two thousand office workers for five years, the researchers found that those who stood up and moved for a few minutes every half hour had about 17% lower risk of developing metabolic problems than colleagues who sat almost without interruption.

Tracking the online and offline behaviour of more than two thousand teenagers for two years, the researchers found that those who spent the most time passively scrolling reported about 42% fewer close friendships, while those who used messaging to arrange real meetings reported more.

Across a review of more than forty studies, students who learned with well-designed game elements scored about 51% higher on tests of the material than those taught in the usual way, and they also reported greater motivation to keep practising.
qs.ex: 细节题。第二段描述了研究结果（设计良好的游戏化学习让测验得分与练习动机更高），其余选项与文中内容不符。

qs.q: What explanation do the researchers offer for the result?
opts: Bikes are most valuable for the awkward middle distances that are too long to walk and too short to justify a car, and their presence at stations encourages people to use rail for the longer part of the journey.
Games work by giving immediate feedback, clear goals and a sense of progress, all of which keep learners in a state of focused effort that traditional exercises often fail to create.
Music appears to work by competing for attention in the brain, drawing mental resources away from pain signals, and slow, familiar tunes also lower anxiety, which itself magnifies pain.

Moderate exercise increases blood flow to the brain and, just as importantly, gives the mind regular breaks from focused attention, and both effects appear to help people see problems from fresh angles.
qs.ex: 推断/因果题。第三段解释了结果背后的机制（即时反馈、明确目标与进步感维持专注投入）。

qs.q: What does the passage suggest that readers do?
opts: Teachers should use game elements that reward understanding and effort, such as levels based on mastery, rather than simple speed or luck-based prizes.
Students facing difficult or lengthy material should consider printing it or using tools that allow highlighting, and they should read actively, pausing to summarise each section.
Managers should praise specific effort, deliver criticism privately, and always end feedback sessions with one or two concrete actions the employee can try before the next meeting.
City authorities should support independent convenience stores through reasonable rents and licensing, and encourage them to stock fresh food alongside quick snacks.
qs.ex: 建议/态度题。末段给出的建议是「奖励应与掌握程度挂钩，避免只为速度与运气的浅层奖励」。

title: 选择过多与决策疲劳，科学怎么说？
sub: 仔细阅读 Section C 实战 · 博浩原创真题风格长文 · 心理话题

data.passage:
Supermarkets routinely offer dozens of brands of jam, cereal and olive oil, and customers are assumed to welcome the abundance. How much does it really matter? A group of researchers at Princeton University set out to examine a familiar but surprisingly unresolved question: Whether having too many choices makes decisions harder rather than better. What the team discovered, described in detail in the British Medical Journal, is worth the attention of anyone who faces this situation regularly.
To answer the question, the researchers designed a study that compared two situations as closely as possible. The results pointed in one direction and were supported by more than one measure. In a famous field experiment repeated with modern data, shoppers faced with a display of about 29 varieties were far more likely to buy nothing than those offered only a handful of options. The pattern held even after the researchers took other possible explanations into account.
Why would such a difference appear? Every additional option demands a little more mental comparison, and when the differences are small, the effort of choosing can exceed the value of any single product. It is a reminder that apparently small choices can have surprisingly large effects.
There is, however, another side to the story. The effect disappears when people already know what they want, and researchers found that expert buyers actually preferred larger assortments because they could scan the range quickly. The researchers stress that the results should be applied with care. As always, one study alone rarely settles a question for good.
What does this mean in practice? Retailers should organise choices into clear categories and highlight a few recommended options, while consumers facing important decisions should limit themselves to a short shortlist. Whether the change is worth making now seems easier to answer than it did before. The evidence, in short, gives people a practical reason to change how they go about their daily routines.

qs.q: What question does the passage set out to answer?
opts: Whether having too many choices makes decisions harder rather than better.
Whether rooftop gardens can meaningfully cool cities and reduce energy use.
How the spread of mobile payment changes the way people manage money.
Whether moving to a four-day week can maintain productivity while improving well-being.

qs.q: What did the study described in the passage find?
opts: In a famous field experiment repeated with modern data, shoppers faced with a display of about 29 varieties were far more likely to buy nothing than those offered only a handful of options.
Examining fish sold in markets around the world, the team found microplastic particles in about 13% of the samples, with the highest concentrations in shellfish that feed close to the shore.

Analysing the results of language tests taken by more than three thousand adult learners, the researchers found that those who began before the age of about ten reached near-native levels more often, but adults who started later and practised daily improved just as fast once they passed the beginner stage.

Combining satellite imagery with temperature readings from hundreds of weather stations, the researchers found that neighbourhoods with dense tree cover were about 6 degrees cooler on hot afternoons and recorded fewer heat-related emergency calls.
qs.ex: 细节题。第二段描述了研究结果（面对几十种同类商品时，顾客购买率明显低于面对少量选择时），其余选项与文中内容不符。

qs.q: What explanation do the researchers offer for the result?
opts: Every additional option demands a little more mental comparison, and when the differences are small, the effort of choosing can exceed the value of any single product.
Second-hand markets extend the useful life of goods and keep them out of landfill, but their green credentials depend on whether the buyer would have bought new anyway.

Cars are parked for most of the day, which makes them unusually flexible loads, and smart chargers that delay charging until demand is low can turn a potential strain on the grid into a useful balancing tool.
Sitting for hours slows the muscles' ability to clear sugar from the blood, and regular movement, even of light intensity, keeps that metabolic machinery running.
qs.ex: 推断/因果题。第三段解释了结果背后的机制（每个选项都要求比较，差异微小时选择成本超过收益）。

qs.q: What does the passage suggest that readers do?
opts: Retailers should organise choices into clear categories and highlight a few recommended options, while consumers facing important decisions should limit themselves to a short shortlist.
Cities should plan for the growth of one-person households by providing smaller housing, shared community spaces and services that make it easy for residents to stay connected.
Procrastinators should break tasks into tiny first steps, commit to starting for just five minutes, and forgive themselves afterwards, since guilt tends to fuel further avoidance.
Platforms should adopt fairer pay formulas that reward safe riding, and regulators should extend accident insurance and rest protections to gig workers regardless of their formal contract type.

title: 关于人工智能与医疗诊断的新证据
sub: 仔细阅读 Section C 实战 · 博浩原创真题风格长文 · 科技话题

data.passage:
Artificial intelligence can now examine medical images and spot patterns that escape the human eye, raising hopes and fears about the future of diagnosis. How much does it really matter? A group of researchers at the University of Oxford set out to examine a familiar but surprisingly unresolved question: How well artificial intelligence performs when it assists rather than replaces doctors. What the team discovered, described in detail in the British Medical Journal, is worth the attention of anyone who faces this situation regularly.
To answer the question, the researchers designed a study that compared two situations as closely as possible. The results pointed in one direction and were supported by more than one measure. In a trial involving thousands of X-rays, doctors who worked alongside an AI system made about 42% fewer diagnostic errors than doctors working alone, while the AI on its own was still less accurate than the best human specialists. To make sure the comparison was fair, the team controlled for factors such as background and daily habits.
What explains the pattern? AI excels at noticing subtle details in images but struggles with the wider context of a patient's history, which is why combining machine consistency with human judgement produces the best results. Similar mechanisms have been identified in other settings as well.
There is, however, another side to the story. Researchers warn that doctors may become overconfident when the machine agrees with them and may fail to notice when it is wrong, so the system must be designed to explain its reasoning. The researchers stress that the results should be applied with care. As always, one study alone rarely settles a question for good.
So what should ordinary readers take away from the study? Hospitals should deploy AI as a second pair of eyes that flags suspicious findings for human review, and they should train doctors to question the tool rather than follow it blindly. In a busy world, such small adjustments can add up to real change over time. In the end, the research suggests that small, deliberate habits can shape outcomes more than most people assume.

opts: How well artificial intelligence performs when it assists rather than replaces doctors.

opts: Drawing on surveys of more than ten thousand residents over a decade, the researchers found that people living alone reported about 37% higher satisfaction with their independence, yet they also visited friends and relatives noticeably less often.

title: 力量训练与老年人：证据、机制与启示
sub: 仔细阅读 Section C 实战 · 博浩原创真题风格长文 · 健康话题

data.passage:
Exercise advice for older adults often focuses on gentle activities such as walking, yet muscles matter more with age, not less. For years the answer has remained surprisingly unclear, so researchers at Seoul National University designed a careful study around a single question: Whether strength training can slow the physical decline associated with ageing. Their findings, published in the American Economic Review, offer one of the clearest answers so far.
The team set out to settle the question with evidence rather than opinion, gathering data over a substantial period. The results pointed in one direction and were supported by more than one measure. In a two-year programme involving hundreds of older adults, those who lifted weights twice a week improved their walking speed and balance by about 16%, and they suffered far fewer falls than a group that did only stretching. Additional checks ruled out the most obvious alternative explanations.
The researchers believe they know why. Strong muscles protect joints, support posture and provide the power needed to catch oneself during a stumble, so rebuilding strength in later life directly reduces the risk of serious injury. The explanation fits with a wider body of research on how the mind works.
There is, however, another side to the story. The researchers emphasise that the training must be progressive and supervised at first, since fragile beginners can injure themselves if they start with weights that are too heavy. The researchers stress that the results should be applied with care. The authors are careful to describe their results as strong evidence rather than final proof.
What does this mean in practice? Older adults should include two short sessions of resistance exercise each week, starting with light weights or body-weight movements and increasing slowly under guidance. The study is a useful reminder that everyday habits matter more than we often assume. And that is a conclusion worth acting on, whatever side of the debate one starts from.

opts: What role public libraries now play in modern communities.

Whether strength training can slow the physical decline associated with ageing.

opts: In a month-long experiment, teams whose meeting load was cut by half reported about 29% higher productivity and produced written work that independent judges rated as significantly better.

title: 外卖骑手的劳动保障，科学怎么说？
sub: 仔细阅读 Section C 实战 · 博浩原创真题风格长文 · 社会话题

data.passage:
Food-delivery platforms have made ordering a meal effortless, but the riders who bring it to the door often work in conditions that attract little public attention. A team of researchers at Princeton University has now added new evidence to the debate, asking a question that is easier to pose than to answer: How the gig economy has changed the nature of work for delivery riders. The results, reported in The Lancet Public Health, may force many people to reconsider long-held assumptions.

Interviewing more than a thousand riders across several cities, the researchers found that about 20% worked more than ten hours a day during peak seasons, yet few had any form of paid leave or accident insurance through their platforms. Some riders told researchers they valued the flexible hours and the chance to earn extra income, but most agreed that basic protections should not depend on their employment status. The researchers stress that the results should be applied with care. As always, one study alone rarely settles a question for good.

Platforms should adopt fairer pay formulas that reward safe riding, and regulators should extend accident insurance and rest protections to gig workers regardless of their formal contract type. Students should divide their revision into short sessions spread over several days or weeks, testing themselves actively rather than simply re-reading notes. In a workplace experiment involving hundreds of junior staff, employees who received feedback focused on specific actions they could take improved about 23% faster than those who received general praise or criticism of their overall performance.

Following more than two thousand office workers for five years, the researchers found that those who stood up and moved for a few minutes every half hour had about 17% lower risk of developing metabolic problems than colleagues who sat almost without interruption.
qs.ex: 细节题。第二段描述了研究结果（边读边回消息的人耗时更长且理解更差），其余选项与文中内容不符。

qs.q: What explanation do the researchers offer for the result?
opts: Sleep appears to help the brain file emotional memories into their proper context, and without that overnight processing, negative images stay vivid and keep intruding into conscious thought.
After a night without food, blood sugar is low, and the brain, which consumes a large share of the body's energy, works noticeably less efficiently until it is replenished.
The brain cannot process two streams of complex information at the same time, so what feels like multitasking is actually rapid switching that carries a hidden cost in time and errors.
People procrastinate not because they are lazy but because the task feels unpleasant or threatening, and avoiding it provides immediate relief that outweighs the distant promise of future reward.
qs.ex: 推断/因果题。第三段解释了结果背后的机制（大脑无法并行处理复杂信息，多任务实为高频切换）。

qs.q: What does the passage suggest that readers do?
opts: Teachers should use game elements that reward understanding and effort, such as levels based on mastery, rather than simple speed or luck-based prizes.
Platforms should adopt fairer pay formulas that reward safe riding, and regulators should extend accident insurance and rest protections to gig workers regardless of their formal contract type.
Procrastinators should break tasks into tiny first steps, commit to starting for just five minutes, and forgive themselves afterwards, since guilt tends to fuel further avoidance.
Students should group related work into blocks, silence their phones during each block, and reserve switching between tasks for genuinely automatic activities.

title: 人脸识别与隐私：一项新研究给出的答案
sub: 仔细阅读 Section C 实战 · 博浩原创真题风格长文 · 科技话题

data.passage:
A glance at a phone screen is now enough to unlock it, and cameras in shops and stations can identify individuals in a crowd within seconds. How much does it really matter? A group of researchers at Seoul National University set out to examine a familiar but surprisingly unresolved question: How comfortable people really are with the spread of facial recognition technology. The results, reported in the Journal of Educational Psychology, may force many people to reconsider long-held assumptions.
To examine the issue, the researchers collected information over time and compared the outcomes with unusual care. The differences that emerged were consistent and difficult to explain away. In a survey of more than five thousand adults, only about 36% said they trusted companies to store their facial data safely, and support for the technology fell sharply when respondents were told that images could be kept for years. The pattern held even after the researchers took other possible explanations into account.
The researchers believe they know why. Faces are unique, permanent and difficult to change, so unlike a password, a stolen facial template cannot simply be replaced once it has been leaked or misused. It is a reminder that apparently small choices can have surprisingly large effects.
There is, however, another side to the story. Support was far higher for limited uses such as unlocking phones or finding missing children, which suggests that public opinion depends less on the technology itself than on who controls it and for how long. The researchers stress that the results should be applied with care. As always, one study alone rarely settles a question for good.
What does this mean in practice? Policymakers should require clear consent, strict time limits on storing facial data and independent oversight before the technology is allowed to spread further. In a busy world, such small adjustments can add up to real change over time. In the end, the research suggests that small, deliberate habits can shape outcomes more than most people assume.

opts: How the spread of mobile payment changes the way people manage money.
How comfortable people really are with the spread of facial recognition technology.
How families can reduce conflict between parents and adolescents.
Whether strength training can slow the physical decline associated with ageing.

qs.q: What did the study described in the passage find?

In a survey of more than five thousand adults, only about 36% said they trusted companies to store their facial data safely, and support for the technology fell sharply when respondents were told that images could be kept for years.
In a famous field experiment repeated with modern data, shoppers faced with a display of about 56 varieties were far more likely to buy nothing than those offered only a handful of options.

opts: Hospitals should offer patients a choice of calming music during procedures and treat it as a low-cost addition to, rather than a replacement for, standard pain relief.

title: 关于孤独与身体健康的新证据
sub: 仔细阅读 Section C 实战 · 博浩原创真题风格长文 · 健康话题

data.passage:
Loneliness is often discussed as an emotional problem, yet doctors increasingly regard it as a medical one. A team of researchers at the University of Oxford has now added new evidence to the debate, asking a question that is easier to pose than to answer: Whether chronic loneliness affects physical health as well as mood. The results, reported in Science Advances, may force many people to reconsider long-held assumptions.
The team set out to settle the question with evidence rather than opinion, gathering data over a substantial period. The differences that emerged were consistent and difficult to explain away. Following nearly nine thousand adults over a period of eight years, the researchers found that those who reported persistent loneliness had about 26% higher risk of developing heart disease, even after controlling for exercise, diet and income. Additional checks ruled out the most obvious alternative explanations.
The researchers believe they know why. Chronic loneliness keeps stress hormones at chronically high levels, which strains the heart and weakens the immune system over many years. The explanation fits with a wider body of research on how the mind works.
There is, however, another side to the story. The researchers distinguish loneliness from simply being alone, since many people who lived by themselves but maintained rich social ties showed no increase in risk. In other words, context matters as much as the practice itself. For that reason, sweeping conclusions should be treated with caution.
For people who face this question every day, the practical message is fairly clear. Health services should routinely ask older patients about their social connections, and communities should invest in affordable meeting places and volunteer programmes that reduce isolation. Whether the change is worth making now seems easier to answer than it did before. In the end, the research suggests that small, deliberate habits can shape outcomes more than most people assume.
